summary: Describes the format and use of RSVP's INTEGRITY object, which provides hop-by-hop integrity and authentication of RSVP messages. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: Each message gets a tamper seal checked at every stop, so nobody can sneak in a fake reservation.

questions: what is the rsvp integrity object
how does rsvp prevent replay attacks
why does rsvp not use ipsec
what is the rsvp integrity handshake
subtitle: Signing every RSVP message at each hop so forged or replayed reservations are rejected.

tldr.problem: RSVP admission control can be abused if messages can be corrupted, forged or replayed, so RSVP needs a way to protect its messages between neighbors.
tldr.mechanism: Each RSVP message carries an INTEGRITY object with a key identifier, a 64-bit increasing sequence number and a keyed message digest (HMAC-MD5 is required). Receivers check the digest and discard messages whose sequence numbers are old.
tldr.outcome: Messages are protected hop by hop against forgery, modification and replay, but not against eavesdropping, because nothing is encrypted. RFC 3097 updates this RFC.

today: RFC 2747 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3097. The text does not say how widely it is deployed.

sections.title: Protecting RSVP Messages
sections.content:
RSVP sets up reservations in routers and hosts, and a reservation depends on admission control and policy rules. To keep that control trustworthy, RFC 2747 protects RSVP messages hop by hop against corruption and spoofing.

The sender attaches an authenticating digest computed with a secret Authentication Key and a keyed-hash algorithm. Each message also carries a one-time-use sequence number so the receiver can spot replays. The mechanism does not give confidentiality: messages stay in the clear. The text notes that this also makes the mechanism exportable from most countries.

Here, "sender" and "receiver" mean the two systems facing each other across one RSVP hop, with the sender being the system that generates the message. The RSVP checksum MAY be set to zero when an INTEGRITY object is present, because the digest is a much stronger check.
sections.eli5: It is like sealing each letter with wax that only your neighbor can check. The letter is still readable, but nobody can swap it without breaking the seal.

sections.title: Why Not IPsec
sections.content:
The working group considered the standard IPsec authentication and rejected it. IPsec security associations are based on destination address, and it is unclear that RSVP messages fit either source or destination based associations. A router must forward PATH and PATH TEAR messages using the sender's address from the SENDER TEMPLATE, and RSVP traffic may not follow the same path as data traffic.

Neighbor relationships can also span non-RSVP clouds that the sending system cannot see. The RFC concludes that key management should be based on RSVP router to RSVP router associations instead.
sections.eli5: The general lock-and-key system did not fit well here, so the designers made a simpler one just for neighbors who talk to each other.

sections.title: The INTEGRITY Object
sections.content:
An RSVP message is a sequence of type-length-value objects. The INTEGRITY object (Class = 4, C-Type = 1) is used for both IPv4 and IPv6 and has four parts.

  • Flags (8 bits): only bit 0, the Handshake Flag (HF), is defined. Senders willing to answer integrity handshakes SHOULD set it to 1; the rest MUST be 0.
  • Key Identifier: an unsigned 48-bit number that MUST be unique for a given sender. Together with the sender's IP address it identifies the security association.
  • Sequence Number: an unsigned 64-bit, monotonically increasing, unique number.
  • Keyed Message Digest: a multiple of 4 octets long; 16 bytes for HMAC-MD5.

The security association records the algorithm and mode, the key, its lifetime, the sending interface and selection criteria, the sender's source address, the latest sequence number sent, and the last N sequence numbers received.
sections.eli5: The seal has a label saying which key was used, a counter that only goes up, and the secret stamp itself.

sections.title: Generating Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
Sequence numbers must be unique for the lifetime of the key and must increase monotonically, modulo 2^64. That lets a receiver keep only the highest number seen. The idea is drawn from TCP. The RFC notes that a 64-bit field would not run out within a year even at an average of about 585 gigaMessages per second, while a 32-bit field would limit the rate to about 136 messages per second.

Surviving a restart needs some stable storage. Three approaches are described.

  • Simple counter: increment per message and save it to stable storage. If it was saved periodically, add the save interval after a restart.
  • Real time clock: use an NTP-style timestamp, filling low bits with a message counter if the clock is coarse.
  • Network recovered clock: if the device has no stable storage, recover the clock from the network using NTP, then proceed as above.
sections.eli5: Each message is numbered like a ticket at a deli counter, and the numbers must never go backwards, even if the shop closes and reopens.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and the Handshake
sections.content:
Messages sent on a secured interface MUST carry an INTEGRITY object. The sender zeroes the RSVP checksum, picks the key by interface (and optionally other criteria), sets the sequence number, zeroes the digest field, computes the digest and writes it in. A receiver on a secured interface discards messages that lack the object, finds the key from the Key Identifier and the sender's address, recomputes the digest and discards the message on a mismatch.

Replay checking is next. A message is valid if its sequence number is greater than the maximum seen, or lies in a reordering window and has not been seen. Implementations SHOULD let administrators configure the window; the RFC's example is 32 messages, and a window of one means no reordering is tolerated.

A restarting receiver MAY run an integrity handshake to learn the sender's current sequence number. It sends an Integrity Challenge (message type 11) with a CHALLENGE object (Class = 64, C-Type = 1) holding a unique cookie. The sender replies with an Integrity Response (type 12) that returns the CHALLENGE and is signed. Receivers SHOULD NOT handshake with senders whose HF is 0.
sections.eli5: If a neighbor forgets what number you were on, it asks a question with a secret word in it. You answer with that word, signed, and so it learns your number again.

sections.title: Key Management and Kerberos
sections.content:
The RFC deliberately leaves out integrated key management, since such protocols have a history of subtle flaws. The Key Identifier is the hook for a future IETF protocol. Each key has a lifetime (KeyStartValid to KeyEndValid), and implementations MUST support more than one key at a time, a specific lifetime per key and manual key distribution.

To change keys without losing state, administrators should overlap the old and new key lifetimes by at least twice the uncertainty in clock synchrony. If the last key expires, the system should notify the network manager and treat the key as having infinite lifetime rather than fall back to no authentication.

Kerberos MAY be used to produce the key. The sender gets a ticket and an ephemeral session key from the KDC and sends the ticket in an Identity Policy Object; the receiver decrypts it to get the same key.
sections.eli5: Keys are like house keys that must be changed now and then. For a while both old and new keys work, so nobody gets locked out.

sections.title: Conformance
sections.content: A conforming implementation MUST support all aspects of the specification. HMAC-MD5 MUST be implemented by all conforming implementations, and others such as SHA MAY be supported. Manual key distribution and smooth key rollover MUST be supported. Implementations SHOULD support a standard key management protocol once the IETF standardizes one.
sections.eli5: Everyone must at least know the same basic secret-stamp trick, so any two routers can understand each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism is believed secure against active and passive attacks, provided the algorithms and keys are strong, implementations are correct, and the keys are kept confidential. The challenge message is intentionally not integrity-checked, so that two peers without starting sequence numbers do not keep dropping each other's challenges. An intruder could therefore forge challenges, save the responses and try to play one back if it guesses the cookie, which is based on a local secret. The RFC calls this very difficult to exploit.

There is no confidentiality and no protection against traffic analysis. The RFC suggests IPsec ESP for confidentiality and bulk link encryption against traffic analysis.
sections.eli5: The seal stops fakes, but a nosy person can still read the letters and see who is writing to whom.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Only bit 0, the Handshake Flag, is defined.

fields.name: Key Identifier
fields.desc: Unique per sender; identifies the key with the sender address.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Monotonically increasing and unique for the key's lifetime.

viz.caption: THE INTEGRITY HANDSHAKE AFTER A RECEIVER RESTART

messages.label: Integrity Challenge (type 11)
messages.note: Carries the Key Identifier and a unique challenge cookie.

messages.label: Integrity Response (type 12)
messages.note: Returns the CHALLENGE object, signed with the key.
